Name: Adam
Transcript: This is our last one. The season's over, more or less. Looking back over the year, what has it been like for you, keeping the plot?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Up and down. Very up and down. The summer was good, mostly, I told you about the summer. The autumn was hard. Work got very busy in September, we had a big system move, three months of planning and it all went wrong in about a day, and I was on it for weeks. Twelve-hour days. And I stopped going to the plot. I didn't decide to stop. I just didn't go, and then I didn't go again, and then it was three weeks. And when I finally went back it had all gone over. The squashes had rotted on the ground, there was bindweed over everything, the beans had gone black on the poles. And I stood there and I felt I'd let it down. Which is ridiculous. It's a plot. It's a rectangle of clay. You can't let a rectangle down.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You felt you'd let it down. What was that like?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: It was the exact feeling from last autumn. Exactly the same. When I couldn't open the laptop. That feeling of, you've dropped everything, everything's on the floor, and everyone can see. I stood on the path looking at the black beans and I had the whole thing come back, the chest, the hands going. Right there next to Des's shed. And the worst bit was the thought that came with it. Which was, see. The calm was fake. All summer, the tomatoes, the mist, that was fake, that was a holiday. This is what you're actually like. You can't even keep a vegetable patch alive.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What did you do?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: I went home. I didn't touch anything. I just turned round and went home and sat in the flat, and I didn't go back for another week. And I half wrote the email to the committee. Dear secretary, due to work commitments I'm no longer able to, and so on. I had it in drafts. And the next Saturday I went down to clear out my shed, so I could hand the key back with the shed empty. That was the plan. Clear the shed, send the email, done. Another thing I'd stopped.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You said, another thing you'd stopped.

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Yeah. That's the pattern, isn't it. Last autumn I stopped work. Before that I stopped going to the climbing wall, I stopped seeing my friends from university, I stopped replying to the group chat. I'm good at starting things. I'm very good at the spreadsheet stage. And then something gets hard and I just quietly stop, and I don't tell anyone, and the thing just closes behind me. Nobody chases you. That's what I'd learned. If you stop quietly enough, nobody chases you.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And then?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: And then there was a note. Pinned to my shed door with a drawing pin. On the back of a seed packet. It said, leeks want lifting before the frost. D. That's all. Leeks want lifting before the frost. And a D. From Des, obviously. And I stood there and read it about five times. And I realised it was the first note anyone had left me in years that wasn't about work. Not a ticket, not an email, not a reminder. Somebody had written something down for me, by hand, about my leeks.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What did you make of the note?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: It wasn't kind, exactly. It wasn't, are you all right, we've missed you. It was practical. Leeks want lifting. But he'd noticed I wasn't there. That's what got me. Somebody noticed I wasn't there and didn't make it a thing. Didn't ask why. Didn't make me explain. Just, here's what needs doing, when you're back. As if I was coming back. As if that was obvious. And I hadn't decided I was coming back, at all. I'd decided the opposite. But the note had decided for me, sort of.

Name: Adam
Transcript: The note had decided for you.

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Sort of. I think if he'd been kind, if he'd written, hope you're okay, I'd have felt worse. I'd have had to reply. I'd have had to be someone who's not okay, in front of Des. But leeks want lifting. That I could do. That was a job. He gave me a job instead of a feeling. I think he knew. I think he's been around a lot of people who stop.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What happened with the leeks?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: I lifted them. Right then, I didn't even clear the shed. Got the fork out and lifted the leeks, and most of them were fine, actually, a bit thin but fine. And Des came over while I was doing it. And I took my headphones out, both of them, and we talked. For about an hour. Leaning on the shed. And it turns out his wife died two years ago. He comes to the plot every day because he needs somewhere to be at, that's how he put it, somewhere to be at. He's been there forty years and the last two he's been there more than ever. And I'd had no idea. I'd been waving at him for eight months and I had no idea.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Somewhere to be at.

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Yeah. He said it like it was obvious. A man needs somewhere to be at. And I thought, that's it, isn't it. That's what the flat isn't, for me. The flat is somewhere I am. It's not somewhere I'm at. I'm at work, in the flat. I'm at my therapist's, on a screen, in the flat. The plot's the only place I go to be at. And Des has known that for forty years and I worked it out in eight months, leaning on a shed. Or he told me, really. He worked it out for me.

Name: Adam
Transcript: No idea.

Name: Arlo
Transcript: None. I'd been treating him like a pop-up. You know, the little box that comes up and you click it away without reading it. Every time he said something I'd take one headphone out and say pardon and click him away. And all that time he'd been doing the thing I said I wanted to do. Being somewhere without anyone needing him to perform. Just being there. And I'd been performing not needing anyone. Very hard. With headphones. I felt quite ashamed of that, actually, standing there with my leeks.

Name: Adam
Transcript: How has it been with Des, since?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Different. Easier. He still talks about the weather, mostly, and onions. But now when he talks about the weather I know he's talking to someone, if you see what I mean. He's not just being polite at the bloke with the headphones. And I go over sometimes now. Not every time. But sometimes I walk over to his shed and stand there while he does something, and he tells me what he's doing, and I don't really listen, and it's fine. He gave me a cutting of his gooseberry. I've no idea what to do with a gooseberry. But I've got one.

Name: Adam
Transcript: In March you said you wanted one problem that nobody can email you about. How is that now?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Yeah. I thought about that, after. Because Des basically emailed me. On paper. He sent me a message about a problem with my leeks, with a deadline, before the frost. It was a ticket. It was literally a ticket. And it was the best thing that happened to me all year. So I don't know what that means. I think it means I didn't want nobody to contact me. I wanted nobody to contact me about things that aren't real. Leeks are real. Des is real. The frost is real. Somebody's server being down at a company I've never visited, I'm less sure.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And the quiet you wanted?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: It comes and goes. It's not a cure. My therapist would like it to be a cure, I think, she'd like to put it in a report. I'd like it to be a cure. It's not. Some days I go down there and my head's as loud as anywhere. But I know where to find it now. That's what's different. A year ago I didn't know there was anywhere to find it. I thought loud was just what my head was. Now I know there's a place, and a time, where it sometimes goes quiet. That's something I didn't have a year ago.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Knowing where to find it. Can you say more?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Tuesday mornings. Early. Doing something fiddly with my hands, tying, or picking beans, something with a bit of attention in it but not too much. No headphones. I've worked that out. It's not a recipe, it doesn't always work. I can't make it happen. But I can go where it happens. I can put myself in the way of it. That's the best way I can say it. I can't switch it on, but I know which room it lives in. And it's never sitting down, by the way. I bought the fold-up chair, in April, the one I told you about. I've never sat in it. It's in the shed with the spider. The quiet never came in the chair. It came with string in my hands.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Does the plot still come up with your therapist?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: No. That's the other thing. I stopped telling her about it in September, just before the work thing. It started to feel like mine. Not homework. I didn't want to hand it in any more. I didn't want her being pleased about it. And then when I stopped going, those three weeks, I didn't tell her that either. Which probably means something. She'd say it means something. I'd say I didn't want to make it a thing. Which is also what Des did with the note. Didn't make it a thing. Maybe I learned it from him.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Will you keep the plot?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Yes. But I'm not sure I want to. That's the honest answer. I think I need it, which is different. Wanting it would be nice. Wanting it would be like, oh, I love my allotment, like a hobby, like people in magazines. I don't love it. Some days I really don't like it at all. But I need it. When I didn't go for three weeks, something went wrong in me. Not in the plot. In me.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You need it rather than want it. Say more about that?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Wanting is nice. Needing is a bit frightening. Because if you need something, you can lose it, and then you're back to, you know, the flat and the queue and the laptop lid. I don't like needing things. I've organised my whole life so I don't need things, I'm very self-sufficient, I do my own tech support. And now I need a rectangle of clay. And here's the odd bit. I think what I needed most this year was something that doesn't care about me at all. The plot doesn't care. It doesn't care if I'm good at it, or calm, or there. It just does its thing. The slugs come. The frost comes. It's the one thing in my life that isn't evaluating me.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And your body this year, looking back?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: My hands, still. The calluses have gone soft a bit, over the three weeks, which annoyed me. And sleep. I sleep better on plot days, that held all year. But here's the thing I noticed. When I stopped going in September, the sleep went first. Before I'd even noticed I'd stopped going, I was lying awake again at three. My body knew before I did. I think it's been keeping a better record than me. My sister says I look less grey. I've decided to take that as a compliment.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Is there anything else, about the year, that I haven't asked about?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: The headphones. In March and July I had them in all the time, I told you. I'd decided I was going to try taking them out next spring. New season, new start, that kind of thing. Very me, scheduling it. But actually, I took them out last week. Without planning it. For about ten minutes. Des was talking about onions, about which onions you put in in the autumn and which you leave till spring. And I just listened. And it was fine. It was quite boring, honestly. Onions are quite boring. But it was fine. It was really fine. I didn't need to mute myself. I just stood there being bored by onions with an old man in the cold. And it was one of the better ten minutes of my year.
